en: How much that criterion matters to you (1-5)

es: Qué tan bien cumple (toca para subir)
en: How well it does on it (tap to raise)

es: Toca un nombre para cambiarlo, el peso para subir lo que te importa ese criterio y cada casilla para puntuar del 1 al 5. El total ya viene multiplicado por los pesos.
en: Tap a name to change it, the weight to raise how much that criterion matters, and each cell to score it from 1 to 5. The total already comes multiplied by the weights.
A mind map opens a topic in every direction: the idea in the middle, the big branches around it and their details hanging off them. It is for emptying your head before settling on any order.
The tree goes from general to specific, like an org chart. Use it when what you have is categories that split into subcategories, not loose ideas.
The etymology tree takes a word apart: where it comes from, what it means, how it is used and which words belong to its family. Handy to dig into a concept before a brainstorm or to name something.
A word taken apart: its origin, meanings, usage and family.
Braces split a whole into its pieces, left to right — the classic outline. Good for taking something apart and seeing what it is made of.
The circle puts a topic in the middle and surrounds it with everything you know about it, with no hierarchy. Handy to explore a concept or to revise before an exam.
The flowchart chains steps with arrows. Tap a step and use the shape button to turn it into a start, a decision or an end: diamonds are the yes/no questions.
The timeline sorts by date: each milestone lands alternately above and below the line, and its details hang outwards. Start the milestone with the year and it reads by itself.
The cycle chains stages that start over. Add each stage from the root — tap the background so it does not hang off the previous one — and they spread around the circle on their own.
The pyramid stacks levels: each one rests on the one below, so the base is what you have to cover first. Tap a level name twice to change it.
The Venn faces two sets off and what they share falls where they overlap. Pick the region in the bottom bar before adding, or drag an item onto another one and it moves by itself.
The comparison puts two topics in columns and what they share in the middle. It is the Venn as a table: quicker to read when there are many points per side.
Every point weighs from 1 to 5: select it and use − + in the bottom bar. Each column adds up at its foot, so the decision stops being “which list is longer”.
The force field looks at a change: what pushes it on the left, what holds it back on the right, each with its weight. If the right-hand side wins, go after the heaviest force first.
Strengths and weaknesses are YOURS; opportunities and threats come from outside. When in doubt, ask yourself whether it depends on you or not.
Important on top, urgent on the left. The “schedule it” quadrant is the one that moves the needle: if it stays empty, you are firefighting all day.
Each branch is an option and its consequences hang from it. Write them down even when they seem obvious: what is not written compares to nothing.
S is the best and D the worst. Whatever you cannot rank yet waits below in “Unranked”: drag it to its row once you are sure.
The head is the problem and each bone a family of causes (method, equipment, materials, measurement…). Look for CAUSES, not solutions: those come later.
One decision in two columns: what adds up and what does not.
Four quadrants: strengths, opportunities, weaknesses and threats.
Fishbone: a problem and the causes behind it.
